tei:titleStmt.tei:title: על אלה אני בוכיה
Ḳinah for the Chmielnicki Massacres of 1648–1649, by Yaaqov Ḳoppel ben Tsvi Margoliyot (1658)

tei:div.tei:head: Ḳinah for the Chmielnicki Massacres of 1648–1649, by Yaaqov Ḳoppel ben Tsvi Margoliyot (1658)

tei:l.tei:note: This is a ḳinnah over the murder of the sages of Polonia.

tei:lg.tei:l: Over these I weep
The wellspring of my eyes pours bitter tears
For the souls of the pious, the pure, and the upright
Whose blood was shed as running water
Killed and slaughtered and burned and stabbed
Leaders and teachers, (regardless their being) elders or youths
Every human heart melts, every spirit and soul falters
They weep and wail without rest
For the wailing voice we heard of pillage and devastation
As those wrapped in sackcloth, covered in ash,
called out to lamenters and learned ones:
“Oy! to us who shall die — here today, the grave tomorrow.”
The lamp of mitsvot and light of Torah, extinguished;
oh! How she now sits humiliated!
Even while the flaming fire burns within the community of Israel,
Is there no-one who can bring the inner meaning of Torah out into light?
I will eulogize and intone laments as mournfully as ostriches do:
Who could listen and not weep and wail tears?
and their body seize with shuddering and trembling
Over the blood of Israel, the treasured people, bleeding out like water?
When pious ones and gatekeepers are nowhere to be found,
what will the simpleton and boorish do?
For the wailing voice we heard of pillage and devastation
as every man’s face turns ashen.
Virgin women, raped, defiled,
hanged by their shrunken breasts.
A target was placed upon them, and arrows flew;
they called out to God until their soul departed.
How are the tents of Ḳedar and Yavan united?
They pined to massacre, as their depravity grew.
Youth and also elder, they set to slaughter.
Where are the fruits of the Faith for them to taste‽
To what land shall I compare you, Poland?
Now that you have turned on us, we have no sanctuary.
These are those who are lashed and stoned:
the Aron haḲodesh is captured, and every precious thing.
Who will join to contain and devour the Devourer?
Who is the one who can say to the angel, “Cease!”?
Excruciating is their lingering departure,
From where will they finally depart?
For those lost we will lament their losses
Shaddai– say our suffering is enough!
Avenge our retribution for us to see.
Avenging the blood of His servants has been foretold:
YHVH El of retribution, appear! (Psalms 94:1)

tei:note.tei:p: viz 2 Samuel 14:14. “We must all die; we are like water that is poured out on the ground and cannot be gathered up. God will not take away the life of one who makes plans so that no one may be kept banished.” — Jacob Chatinover
Possibly כָּמַ֣הּ (as in Psalms 63:2) – “faint, as with longing”. matches כָהֲתָ֥ה (as in Deuteronomy 34:7) “falter/grow weak.” –Jacob Chatinover
An image that appears a few times, the language here is most similar to Psalms 106:18.

I think this must be “ki-venot ya`ana” as in Mikhah 1:8. Benot ya`ana are ostriches (or usually translated as such), and in addition to the quote from Mikhah they appear in other spots, usually with jackals, as symbols of desolation (Isaiah 43:20, Isaiah 34:13; Job 30:29; without jackals but as symbols of desolation in Isaiah 13:21 and Jeremiah 50:39). — Jacob Chatinover.

Parur is a type of pot (Numbers 11:8, others). But the word “qibbtsu” appears twice (out of five total in Tanakh) in this phrase: קבּצו פארוּר (Nah 2:11, Joel 2:6) both time with “panim“, meaning basically for a face to turn ashen. So maybe it’s supposed to be with an alef, but there’s also a suggestion of mutilating/decapitating faces (taking trophies of noses?) and collecting them in a pot. –Jacob Chatinover

Apocalyptic reference to combative tribal powers. For Yavan, often referred to as an eponymous ancestor of the Greeks, find Daniel 8:21-22 and Daniel 11:2. For Ḳedar, Genesis 25:13 and 1 Chronicles 1:29.
Possibly referencing the folk etymology of “Polin” as “po” (here) lin” (we will lodge). –Jacob Chatinover
BT Ketubot 104a, on the death of Rebbi Yehuda haNasi.
Cf. “מחמד עין” as in Lam 2:4, Ezekiel 24:16, Ezekiel 24:21, Ezekiel 24:25, 1 Kings 20:6, each time in the context of a threat of things being taken away or destroyed. –Jacob Chatinover
1 Kings 20:14: “He asked, ‘Who shall begin the battle?’ And he answered, ‘You.'” ye’sor means “to hitch up”, used for a chariot, a gartel, or metaphorically to join battle.
A reference to Yaakov’s wrestling with the angel/ish.
Note play between “pri datam” in the previous stanzas and “phridatam” here.
Playing with the midrashic etymology of Shaddai as “zeh she’amar ‘Dai!’ le`olamo”, viz Pirkei dRebi Eliezer 3:7, Bereshit Rabba 5:8. –Jacob Chatinover
